title: ever-rising spirits
hookLine: ever-rising spirits — optimism as a discipline
tomorrow: what a sikh carries and why

cards: Ask a Sikh grandfather how he's doing. He's eighty-one, his knees are bad, and the doctor's news this week wasn't great. There's a decent chance he'll smile and say two words: chardi kala.
Not I'm fine. Something more like: spirits rising. He's noticed everything.
He's just decided which way his spirit is going to face.

teach.b: Chardi kala. Chardi means rising, climbing. Kala means spirit, energy, a state of being.
Ever-rising spirits. Here's the difference between chardi kala and just being cheerful.

teach.h: NOT CHEERFULNESS. IT HOLDS WHEN THINGS FALL.
teach.b: Cheerfulness depends on circumstances. Chardi kala is meant to hold when circumstances collapse. And Sikh history has asked a great deal of it.
There were long stretches, especially in the eighteenth century, when Sikhs were hunted, driven into forests and hills.
Out of those years came a whole defiant way of speaking: tradition remembers that a lone Sikh might call himself sava lakh, a hundred and twenty-five thousand. One man, a whole army.
Not denial: a refusal to let circumstances write your spirit for you. Where does it come from? From trust.

teach.h: TRUST IN HUKAM, THE WILL OF GOD.
teach.b: Sikhs speak of hukam, the will of God running through everything. If all of life, even the hard parts, is held inside the one, despair doesn't get the last word.
You heard the phrase on day five: the Ardas asks for it near its very end. And chardi kala doesn't forbid sadness. Sikhs grieve, and weep.
It just keeps pointing up, like a plant that grows toward the light in a dark room.

how: Sikhs speak of chardi kala in everyday greetings and answers, and ask for it at the close of the Ardas prayer; it is taught as a lasting optimism rooted in trust in God's will.

games.q: what's inside the word — tap the pairs.
p: the will of God running through all

s: chardi kala means pretending everything is fine
Sikhs grieve and weep. chardi kala keeps pointing up without denying the pain.
the phrase appears near the end of the Ardas
the communal prayer asks that the name and the spirit be ever-rising.
chardi kala only works when life is going well
it's meant to hold exactly when circumstances collapse.

games.q: you're a Sikh in the eighteenth century, hiding in the hills with a price on your head. someone asks how you are. what do you say?
games.why: those years produced a whole defiant way of speaking; tradition remembers a lone Sikh calling himself sava lakh, a hundred and twenty-five thousand.

practice: Let one heavy thing come to mind, something that's actually hard right now. Don't push it away.

Then, without denying any of it, let your posture rise a little: lift your chest, soften your face, breathe in as if drawing yourself upward. You're not saying it's fine. You're choosing which way your spirit faces.
Stay there, with the weight and the rising together.

wordCard.voice: Chardi kala. Ever-rising spirits: hope practiced as a discipline, holding even when life is hard. Seventeenth word.

orig.note: Punjabi, in Gurmukhi script: chardi (rising) + kala (spirit, energy).

carryVoice: Your line: rise anyway. Not pretending it's fine; just choosing which way to face. Day seventeen.
